4 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Embedded system definition An embedded system is a microprocessor-based computer hardware system with software that is designed to perform a dedicated function, either as an independent system or as a part of a large system. Limited resources: • Processing • Memory • Peripherals

# Page 6^page=6
6 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Development platform The programmer and debugger interface facilitates bi-directional communication between the host (PC) and the microcontroller. It allows the user to perform real-time debugging directly on the microcontroller by: • Pausing execution. • Inspecting and modifying memory and registers. • Setting breakpoints to halt execution at specific code locations. • Single-stepping through instructions to observe behavior.

7 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Example of a development platform

# Page 8^page=8
8 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Microcontroller definition A microcontroller is a microprocessor (CPU) with added functionality, such as memory and peripheral hardware.

# Page 9^page=9
9 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems CPU and memories and peripherals CPU (Central Processing Unit) = core of the microcontroller that executes instructions and controls system operations: • Executes program instructions • Performs calculations (ALU) • Controls peripherals and data flow • Manages interrupts Memories • Flash: non-volatile, stores the program • RAM: volatile, stores variables and temporary data

# Page 10^page=10
10 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Peripherals = hardware modules inside a MCU that perform a specific function independently of the CPU (CPU and peripherals work in parallel). Peripherals are connected to CPU via internal buses. Peripherals interacts with the external world or handle internal tasks. • Communication: I2C, SPI, USART... • Timing: clocks, PWM… • Analog signal processing: ADC, DAC… • General Purpose Input/Output (GPIO) • Power management

# Page 13^page=13
13 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems RISC vs CISC ARM = Advanced RISC Machine RISC: Reduced Instruction Set Computer Based on very simple instructions that execute within a single cycle, at high clock speed. CISC: Complex Instruction Set Computer Based on more complex instructions to complete a task in as few lines as possible. VS Example: how to execute 1800 + 1801 CISC ADD 1800, 1801 RISC Load X, 1800 Load Y, 1801 ADD X, Y Store 1800, X Memory locations

# Page 14^page=14
14 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems RISC vs CISC CISC • Little work from the compiler to pass from high-level language into assembly (and little memory needed) • Short codes • More clock cycles • More difficult pipeline • More transistors used to store instructions RISC • Long codes and more RAM needed (and it must also be fast) • More general purpose hardware • One cycle per instruction (or even less) • Easier pipeline • More transistors used for register memories

# Page 15^page=15
15 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems ARM IP model and families • A: application (high-end) • R: real time (more focus on timing performance) • M: more wide-range and mainstream Business model: Intellectual Property Licensing

17 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems ARM-Cortex pipelining 2-level (M0+) 3-level (M3/4) Fetch&Decode Decode&Execute Fetch&Decode Decode&Execute Fetch&Decode Decode&Execute Fetch Decode Execute Fetch Decode Execute Fetch Decode Execute

# Page 18^page=18
18 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems ARM-Cortex pipelining Fetch Decode Execute Fetch Decode Execute Fetch Decode Execute • Fetch: the processor fetches (picks) the instruction from memory (usually from flash or RAM) and loads it into the instruction register. • Decode: the fetched instruction is decoded to determine what kind of operation needs to be performed. • Execute: the instruction is executed, meaning the actual operation (e.g., an arithmetic operation, data transfer, or branching) is carried out.

# Page 19^page=19
19 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems ARM-Cortex M4 memory map 4 GB addressable memory

# Page 20^page=20
20 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems ARM-Cortex M4 memory map Code (0x00000000 - 0x1FFFFFFF) Where the program code is stored. It is a Flash memory (non-volatile), meaning the contents are preserved when power is off. SRAM (0x20000000 - 0x3FFFFFFF) Static RAM (SRAM), used for storing variables, data, and stack information during the execution of a program. It is volatile. No need to be constantly refreshed, unlike DRAM, so: • Faster • Easier to use • Less consumption • More expensive Peripheral (0x40000000 - 0x5FFFFFFF) Reserved for the microcontroller's peripherals, such as timers, ADCs (analog-to-digital converters), DACs (digital-to-analog converters), and communication interfaces like UART, SPI, and I2C.

# Page 21^page=21
2. Exceptions, Interrupts, and Faults 02

# Page 22^page=22
22 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Code Flow in ARM Microcontrollers Reset main() while(1) main loop • Main loop runs continuously in the CPU ISR Interrupt Service Routine while(1) { instruction main 1 instruction main 2 instruction main 3 instruction main 4 ... } interrupt { instruction int 1 instruction int 2 ... } • Interrupts handle asynchronous events from the peripherals • CPU temporarily pauses execution of the main and manages the interrupt in the Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) • After ISR → returns to main loop

# Page 23^page=23
23 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems ARM-Cortex M4 exceptions and interrupts The ARM-cortex M4 features both exceptions and interrupts. Both are handled by the Nested Vectored Interrupt Controller (NVIC). Nested Vectored Interrupt Controller (NVIC)

# Page 24^page=24
24 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems ARM-Cortex M4 exceptions and interrupts Exception sources: • Reset → Processor startup or restart; enters privileged Thread mode • NMI → Non-maskable interrupt with the highest priority after Reset. • HardFault → Severe fault occurring during exception processing. • MemManage → Memory protection violation during instruction or data access. • BusFault → Error during an instruction or data transfer on the memory bus. • UsageFault → Instruction execution error, e.g. undefined instruction, unaligned access, division by zero. • SVCall → Software-generated exception used to request OS/kernel services. • PendSV → System-level service request, mainly used for context switching in an RTOS. • SysTick → System timer exception, commonly used to generate a periodic system tick. • IRQ (Interrupt Request) → Interrupt request generated by a peripheral.

# Page 25^page=25
25 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Interrupts Interrupts can be generated by: • MCU peripherals (Timers, ADC…) • External events (EXTI) → changes in GPIO pins Nested Interrupt Vector (NVIC) manages the interrupt priorities while(1) { instruction main 1 instruction main 2 instruction main 3 instruction main 4 ... } P1 interrupt { instruction int 1 instruction int 2 ... } P1 or P2 interrupt { instruction int 1 instruction int 2 ... } P0 interrupt { instruction int 1 instruction int 2 ... }

# Page 26^page=26
26 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems ARM-Cortex M4 interrupt vector Exception priorities: lower priority number = higher priority Vector Table: stores the starting addresses of all exception handlers.

31 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems STM32F401RE

# Page 32^page=32
32 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Clocks 3 clock sources for system clock (SYSCLK): • HSI oscillator clock • HSE oscillator clock • Main PLL (Phase-Locked Loop) clock. 2 secondary clock sources: • a 32 kHz low-speed internal RC (LSI RC) • a 32.768 kHz low-speed external crystal (LSE crystal) Each source can be switched on/off independently when not used

# Page 33^page=33
33 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Timers Timer modules include: • reference clock (internal or external) • prescaler (reduce the clock frequency) • counter (up, down, up/down mode) • comparison registers Timer modules are used for: • generating interrupts • generating pulse trains • driving Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) outputs • measuring pulse length of input signals • counting events

# Page 34^page=34
36 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems GPIOs A GPIO is a configurable pin used to read or write digital signals. Modes: • Input → read external analog or digital signals (e.g., buttons, analog voltages…) • Output → drive analog or digital signals (e.g., LEDs, analog reference voltages…) • Alternate Function → used by peripherals (e.g., UART, SPI, Timers, etc.)

# Page 35^page=35
39 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Graphical User Interface (GUI)

# Page 36^page=36
40 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems ADC Analog to Digital Converters (ADC): • 12-bit ADC • 19 multiplexed channels Can be triggered by timers. Can be used in interrupt (IT) mode and DMA mode.

# Page 37^page=37
43 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Direct Memory Access (DMA) Hardware unit for high speed data transfer: • peripherals memory • memory memory without the intervention of the CPU → CPU can continue to process the instructions without interruptions

# Page 38^page=38
44 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Communication I2C: 2 wire synchronous communication (SCK, SDA) • 3 I2C bus interfaces can operate in multi-master and slave modes. • Can support the standard (up to 100 kHz) and fast (up to 400 kHz) modes. SPI: 4 wire synchronous full-duplex communication • 4 SPI interfaces USART: asynchronous single-wire half-duplex communication • 3 USART interfaces

# Page 39^page=39
45 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems STM32 programming LL Low-Level drivers: ✓ Better optimization → improved performance × Less portability × Require deep knowledge of the MCU and peripheral specifications HAL Hardware Abstraction Layer drivers: ✓ Hide the MCU and peripheral complexity ✓ Maximize software portability across different microcontrollers ✓ Exist for all peripherals × Larger overhead → performance penalty Both can be found in the “Description of STM32F4 HAL and LL drivers” user manual.

3. NUCLEO board 03

# Page 41^page=41
47 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems NUCLEO board features • Connector for Arduino Uno Revision 3 • General purpose connector (ST morpho extension) male pin headers accessible on both side of the board full access to STM32 I/Os • 3 LEDs: o LD1 (COM) for USB communication (green, red) o LD2 available for user (connected to PA5) (green) o LD3 MCU powered, +5V power is available (red) • 2 pushbuttons: o B1 for USER connected to PC13 o B2 for RESET • LSE (low-speed external) oscillator at 32.768 kHz • 3 interfaces supported by the USB (Virtual Com port, Mass storage, Debug port)

# Page 42^page=42
48 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems NUCLEO board features Information about the NUCLEO board can be found in: • The NUCLEO board datasheet • The NUCLEO board user manual

50 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems POLIMI expansion board

51 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems POLIMI board features • standard 16x2 LCD alphanumeric module • 5x7 LEDs array area, driven by two shift registers connected to the SPI interface • 4x4 keypad, connected directly to the GPIOs • incremental encoder • microphone and comparator • amplifier and speaker, connected to PWM • RGB led, connected to three PWM-configurable outputs • light sensor connected to ADC • potentiometer connected to ADC • thermometer, which communicates through I2C peripheral • accelerometer, which communicates through I2C peripheral • IR led and IR receiver

# Page 47^page=47
53 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems How do we find to which MCU pin something is connected? We need to use two schematics: 1. NUCLEO schematic 2. POLIMI board schematic We will need to identify the sensor we are interested in on the POLIMI board schematic and to find where it is connected to the NUCLEO board. Then, by looking at the NUCLEO schematic, we will identify the STM32F401RE pin we need to use in our code. Try to find: - The Blue Button pin (mounted directly on the NUCLEO) - The microphone pin (mounted on the POLIMI board)
